阿哥哥鈴,Agogo,鼓與打擊樂器,非洲／西非（奈及利亞）／巴西,樂器教學,世界: Agogo,Agogo,Membranophones & percussion,Africa / West Africa (Nigeria) / Brazil,instrument teaching,world instruments,instrument introduction
阿哥哥鈴可見於西非奈及利亞約魯巴音樂，尤其伊佩塞鼓合奏，用於伊法節慶與安撫神祇儀: The agogo appears in Yoruba music of West Africa, especially in the ipeṣe drum ensemble, at Ifá festivals and in rites to appease the deities, and it also appears in subgenres such as jùjú, Afro-jùjú, apala and fuji. In Brazil it is used in Candomblé rites, as accompaniment to capoeira, and in choro ensembles; it is also common in samba baterias and carnival rhythms, where popular musicians use it to shape Afro-Brazilian rhythms, and it appears as a special effect in improvised dance music or Latin suites.
阿哥哥鈴為體鳴樂器，發聲體是兩個大小不同、音高不同的金屬錐形鈴。來源記載其原以鍛: The agogo is an idiophone whose sounding body is two metal cone-shaped bells of different size and pitch. The source records that it was originally made of wrought iron and is now made in many metals and sizes; the metal bell is a fan of sheet iron rolled into a cone, and the two bells are welded to a U-shaped piece of metal or joined by a bent iron rod. It is struck with a drumstick, or with a wooden or metal beater. The materials of the other parts are not stated.
阿哥哥鈴起源於西非音樂，愛多、伊多馬、伊加拉與約魯巴人用它指單鈴或雙鈴。其名稱與: The agogo comes from West African music; the Edo, Idọma, Igala and Yoruba use the word for a single or a double bell. Its name and the knowledge of making it were carried to the Americas by enslaved West Africans. In Nigeria it entered the drum ensemble of Ifá ritual and the music of jùjú, apala and fuji. Once in Brazil it was used in Candomblé rites, in capoeira, and in the choro ensembles of the 1920s, where it played an important part; later it entered samba baterias and carnival, becoming the percussion instrument that shapes Afro-Brazilian rhythms in popular music. Its making also moved from wrought iron to many metals and sizes.
阿果果雙鈴為體鳴鈴類，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號111.242，源自: The agogo double bell is an idiophone of the bell type, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.242, from West Africa and Nigeria and later found in Brazil. It is played holding the U-shaped handle in one hand with the palm against it, the mouths of the two bells facing outwards, the small bell above and the large one below; the two bells are struck with a drumstick or a wooden or metal beater to sound different pitches. The long bell sounds lower and the short one higher; thick walls vibrate less and thin walls vibrate more readily. A beginner first settles the hold and the order of strokes, then practises alternating high and low.
